items.title: 12.2.9 If theta is measured in radian, then Lim_{theta->0} sin(theta)/theta = 1.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
This is the most important limit of trigonometry. Substituting \(\theta = 0\) gives \(\frac{0}{0}\), and no algebra can cancel the \(\theta\), so the book proves it with a figure and the Sandwich Theorem (12.2.8).
"Measured in radian" matters: in radians the arc of a unit circle equals the angle, which is why \(\sin\theta\) and \(\theta\) become almost equal for small angles. In degrees the limit would be \(\frac{\pi}{180}\), not 1.

blocks.caption: Our table (not in the book): the ratio approaches 1 as the angle shrinks

blocks.text: Proof: To evaluate this limit, we apply a new technique. Take \(\theta\) be positive acute central angle of a circle with radius \(r = 1\). As shown in the figure, \(OAB\) represents a sector of a circle. Join \(A\) and \(B\) and extend \(OB\) to \(D\) such that \(OA \perp AD\). Also draw \(BC \perp OC\) on \(OA\).

blocks.alt: Sector OAB of a circle with centre O and radius 1 (r = 1 marked on OB and on OA), angle theta at O. OB is extended to D with AD perpendicular to OA, so triangle OAD is right-angled at A. BC is perpendicular to OA with a right-angle mark at C, and the chord BA is drawn.
blocks.caption: Figure: sector OAB of the unit circle with triangles OAB and OAD (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text:
Given \(|OA| = |OB| = 1\) (radii of unit circle).
In the right \(\Delta OCB\),
\[\sin\theta = \dfrac{|BC|}{|OB|} = |BC|\]
In the right \(\Delta OAD\),
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{|AD|}{|OA|} = |AD|\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why these two lengths? In a unit circle the hypotenuse \(OB\) and the side \(OA\) are both 1, so the opposite sides are exactly \(\sin\theta = |BC|\) and \(\tan\theta = |AD|\). The figure turns the three numbers \(\sin\theta\), \(\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) into three areas.

(i) Area of \(\Delta OAB\)
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}|OA||BC| = \dfrac{1}{2}(1)(\sin\theta)\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\theta\]
(ii) Area of sector \(OAB\)
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}(1)(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2}\theta\]
and
(iii) Area of \(\Delta OAD\)
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}|OA||AD| = \dfrac{1}{2}(1)(\tan\theta)\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\tan\theta\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Area (ii) uses the sector formula \(\frac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta\), which is valid only when \(\theta\) is in radians. Triangle \(OAB\) has base \(OA = 1\) and height \(BC = \sin\theta\); triangle \(OAD\) has base \(OA = 1\) and height \(AD = \tan\theta\).

From the figure we see that
Area of \(\Delta OAB\) < Area of sector \(OAB\) < Area of \(\Delta OAD\)
\[\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\theta < \dfrac{\theta}{2} < \dfrac{1}{2}\tan\theta\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why this order? Triangle \(OAB\) lies inside the sector (the chord \(AB\) is inside the arc), and the sector lies inside triangle \(OAD\). A region inside another has a smaller area.

As \(\sin\theta\) is positive, so on division by \(\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta\), we get
\[1 < \dfrac{\theta}{\sin\theta} < \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \quad \left(0 < \theta < \dfrac{n}{2}\right)\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The range of \(\theta\) is printed as \(0 < \theta < \frac{n}{2}\). It should be
\[0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
(\(\theta\) is a positive acute angle).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Dividing each part by the positive number \(\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta\) keeps the signs \(<\):
\[\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\tan\theta}{\frac{1}{2}\sin\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta/\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\]
Then taking reciprocals of positive numbers reverses each sign, which gives the next line.

Since \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\) is sandwiched between 1 and a quantity approaching 1 itself. So, by the sandwich theorem, it must also approach 1, that is,
\[\lim_{\theta \to 0}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why does the Note hold? \(\frac{\sin(-\theta)}{-\theta} = \frac{-\sin\theta}{-\theta} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\), so the ratio has the same values for negative angles. Hence both one-sided limits are 1, and the limit is 1.

blocks.title: Example 8
steps:
Given: \(\frac{\sin 7\theta}{\theta}\) as \(\theta \to 0\).
To find: the limit.
Method: substituting \(\theta = 0\) gives \(\frac{0}{0}\). The expression looks like \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\), but the angle is \(7\theta\) while the denominator is \(\theta\). Change the variable so that the angle and the denominator match, then use \(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\).

Step 1: Change the variable
\[\text{Let } x = 7\theta, \text{ so that } \theta = \dfrac{x}{7}\]
When \(\theta \to 0\), we have \(x \to 0\).
Why: the standard result needs the same quantity inside the sine and in the denominator. Calling the angle \(x\) makes this possible, and since \(x = 7\theta\), \(x\) also goes to 0.

Step 2: Rewrite the limit
\[\lim_{\theta \to 0}\dfrac{\sin 7\theta}{\theta} = \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\sin x}{\frac{x}{7}}\]
\[= 7\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\sin x}{x}\]
Why: dividing by \(\frac{x}{7}\) is the same as multiplying by \(\frac{7}{x}\); the constant 7 comes outside the limit (Theorem on limits: limit of a constant times a function).

Step 3: Use the standard limit
\[= (7)(1) = 7\]
Why: \(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\) (12.2.9).

Check:
Take a small angle \(\theta = 0.01\) radian: \(\frac{\sin 0.07}{0.01} = \frac{0.069943}{0.01} \approx 6.994\), very close to 7.

blocks.title: Example 9
steps:
Given: \(\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta}\) as \(\theta \to 0\).
To find: the limit.
Method: substituting gives \(\frac{1-1}{0} = \frac{0}{0}\). Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate \(1 + \cos\theta\) to turn \(1 - \cos\theta\) into \(\sin^{2}\theta\), so that \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\) appears.

Step 1: Multiply by the conjugate
\[\dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta} = \dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta}\cdot\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta}\]
\[= \dfrac{1-\cos^{2}\theta}{\theta(1+\cos\theta)}\]
Why: \((1-\cos\theta)(1+\cos\theta) = 1 - \cos^{2}\theta\) (difference of squares). Multiplying by \(\frac{1+\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta} = 1\) does not change the value.

Step 2: Use \(\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1\)
\[= \dfrac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\theta(1+\cos\theta)}\]
\[= \sin\theta\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{1+\cos\theta}\right)\]
Why: \(1 - \cos^{2}\theta = \sin^{2}\theta\). Splitting \(\sin^{2}\theta = \sin\theta \cdot \sin\theta\) lets one \(\sin\theta\) pair with \(\theta\) to make the standard ratio.

Step 3: Take the limit of each factor
\[\lim_{\theta \to 0}\left(\dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta}\right)\]
\[= \lim_{\theta \to 0}\sin\theta\cdot\lim_{\theta \to 0}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\cdot\lim_{\theta \to 0}\dfrac{1}{1+\cos\theta}\]
\[= (0)(1)\left(\dfrac{1}{1+1}\right) = 0\]
Why: the limit of a product is the product of the limits (all three exist). \(\sin 0 = 0\), \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} \to 1\), and \(\cos 0 = 1\), so the last factor is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

Check:
Take \(\theta = 0.01\): \(\frac{1 - \cos 0.01}{0.01} = \frac{0.0000500}{0.01} = 0.005\), which is close to 0 and gets smaller as \(\theta\) gets smaller.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\lim_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1\) (\(\theta\) in radians).
2. Proof: area of \(\Delta OAB\) < area of sector < area of \(\Delta OAD\), i.e. \(\sin\theta < \theta < \tan\theta\), then the Sandwich Theorem.
3. General form: \(\lim_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\sin k\theta}{\theta} = k\) (make the denominator match the angle).
4. For \(1 - \cos\theta\), multiply by \(1 + \cos\theta\) to get \(\sin^{2}\theta\).
5. \(\lim_{\theta \to 0}\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta} = 0\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Cancelling: \(\frac{\sin 7\theta}{\theta} = \sin 7\). "sin" is not a number multiplying \(\theta\); it cannot be cancelled.
2. Writing \(\lim_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\sin 7\theta}{\theta} = 1\). The angle and the denominator must be the same before the result gives 1.
3. Using degrees: the result \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} \to 1\) is true only for radians.
